package.script: An electric eel can zap you with 600 volts. But how? That's five times your wall outlet, and there's no battery inside. Its body is the battery. Most of that long body is packed with special cells called electrocytes. Each one makes a tiny charge, less than a fifth of a volt. Alone, that's nothing. But they're stacked in rows, thousands of them, head to tail, like batteries in a flashlight. When the eel spots a fish, its brain fires one signal, and every cell flips on at once. About six thousand tiny charges add up to one giant shock. Zap! The fish freezes on the spot. Here's the twist: an electric eel isn't even an eel. It's a knifefish, closer to a catfish. So if your body were a battery, what would you power first?
key_facts: The shock comes from the Main and Hunter's organs: some 5,000 to 6,000 stacked electroplaques (electrocytes), working like a battery (Fluke); script says 'about six thousand'
Each electrocyte makes only about 0.15 volt (Fluke); script says 'less than a fifth of a volt', screen shows 0.15 V
A motor-neuron signal opens ion channels so each cell becomes a dipole, and many cells firing together add up to a strong shock (Science ABC)
Electric eels reach about 600 volts (Fluke: up to 500 V; record before 2019 was 650 V; E. voltai measured 860 V, FAPESP); US wall outlet is 120 V, so 600 V = 5x
The electric organ fills most of the body (about two-thirds per Science ABC; script says 'most of that long body')
Electric eels are not true eels: they are knifefishes, more closely related to catfish and carp (FAPESP, Science ABC)

package.pinned_comment: Claws, hairs or the non-stick coating: which spider trick would you steal? 🕷️
package.hook_text: Spider glue almost never lets a fly go. So why do you never see the spider stuck?
package.script: Spider glue almost never lets a fly go. So why do you never see the spider stuck? Secret one: most of the web isn't sticky. The spokes are dry silk. Only the spiral has beads of glue, so the spider walks the spokes. Secret two: its feet. Web spiders have three claws per foot. Insects get two. The extra claw hooks a single thread, like a tiny hand. But here's the wild part. Building one web, a spider touches its own glue hundreds of times. Its legs are covered in branched hairs, so the glue slides along them and drips off. Scientists washed spider legs, and they stuck more. So there's a non-stick coating, too. A fly hits lots of glue at once. The spider barely touches a drop. So which trick would you steal: the claws, the hairs, or the coating?
key_facts: Orb webs: the radial spokes are dry silk, only the spiral carries glue droplets (How It Works; Burke Museum: webs have many non-sticky threads)
Web-building spiders have a third tarsal claw that grips single threads; insects have at most two (Burke Museum)
Briceno & Eberhard 2012 (Naturwissenschaften, STRI/Univ. of Costa Rica): orb weavers touch their sticky silk hundreds to thousands of times while building one web
Branched hairs on the legs let glue droplets slide along and drip off; washing legs with hexane made them stick more, showing a non-stick coating (Smithsonian / phys.org)
Spiders tiptoe around the glue and touch few droplets, while a fly hits many at once (Burke Museum, Vollrath & Tillinghast 1992)

That's more than a billion insects for every single person. Over a million kinds have names, and millions more are still waiting for one. So when they all disappear, they leave a gigantic hole. Start with the flowers. Nearly nine out of ten flowering plants need animals to carry their pollen, and most of those animals are insects. Bees, flies, beetles, moths and butterflies move pollen from flower to flower, so the plant can make seeds and fruit. Without them, the flowers still bloom, but most never turn into fruit. About three quarters of our main food crops get help from pollinators. Apples, almonds, blueberries, cherries and melons would become rare and very expensive. And chocolate? Cacao flowers are pollinated by tiny flies called midges, about the size of a pinhead. No midges, almost no chocolate. Next come the animals that eat insects. Most songbirds feed their chicks on bugs, even the ones that eat seeds as adults. One pair of chickadees needs six to nine thousand caterpillars to raise a single nest of chicks. Bats, frogs, lizards and spiders lose their dinner too. In rivers, trout and many other fish eat young mayflies and caddisflies. Take away the bugs, and the food chain crumbles from the bottom up. Now for the gross part. Insects are nature's cleanup crew. Beetles and fly larvae break down dead leaves, dead animals, and poop. Australia found this out the hard way. When settlers brought cattle, the local dung beetles couldn't handle cow pats. The pats sat in the fields for months, smothering the grass and breeding swarms of flies. So scientists shipped in dung beetles from abroad, and about twenty-three kinds settled in. Now picture that problem everywhere on Earth. Fungi and bacteria would keep working, but much more slowly. So, would humans starve? Not right away. Wheat, rice and corn are pollinated by the wind, so we'd still have bread, rice and popcorn. But our plates would get very boring, and we'd lose honey, silk, and lots of fruits and vegetables. Many wild plants would slowly fade away, and the animals that eat them would follow. Even the soil would suffer, because insects dig it, mix it and feed it. So the next time a bee buzzes past your head, remember, that tiny bug helps keep your whole plate full. Next time: how a bear hunt gave us the teddy bear.

package.title: Why Do Onions Make You Cry After 30 Seconds? 🧅
package.description:
Why do onions make you cry? Cutting an onion mixes a sulfur compound with an enzyme, and a second enzyme (found in 2002) turns the result into syn-propanethial-S-oxide, an irritating gas that peaks about 30 seconds after the cut and makes your tear glands wash it away.

package.pinned_comment: Would you still eat a plant that fights back with tear gas? 🧅 Yes or no?
package.script: Onions fire tear gas at your eyes, 30 seconds after you cut them. How? Inside every onion cell, two chemicals are kept apart, in separate little rooms. One is a sulfur molecule. The other is an enzyme. Your knife smashes the walls, and they finally mix. The enzyme turns the sulfur into an acid, then a second enzyme, only discovered in 2002, flips that acid into a gas. It drifts up, and peaks about 30 seconds after the cut. When it hits your eyes, tiny nerves shout "burning!" So your tear glands flood your eyes, to wash it away. Why bother? It's armor. Any animal that bites an onion, gets a face full of sting. Want fewer tears? Cut it under running water. So, would you still eat a plant that fights back with tear gas?

The tear-causing compound peaks about 30 seconds after the onion is cut
Corneal nerve endings sense it as burning and tear glands wash it away
Cutting under running water reduces exposure

topic.title: How can an owl turn its head almost all the way around?

package.title: How Do Owls Turn Their Heads 270°? 🦉
package.description:
How can an owl turn its head 270 degrees without cutting off blood to its brain? Owls have tube-shaped eyes locked in their skulls, 14 neck bones instead of our 7, arteries that run through bony tunnels up to ten times wider than the vessel, and blood pools at the base of the head that keep the brain fed while it turns.

package.script: You'd black out, but owls spin their heads 270 degrees. How? First, an owl's eyes can't move. They're shaped like tubes, locked inside the skull. So to look around, the whole head has to turn. Second, extra bones. You have seven neck bones. An owl has fourteen, so the twist is shared out, a little at every joint. Third, the clever part: blood. Twisting would pinch the arteries, but an owl's run through bony tunnels, up to ten times wider than the vessel, so they don't get squeezed. And at the base of the head, the vessels balloon into little pools, storing extra blood for the brain, while the head is turned. So, if you had an owl's neck, what's the first thing you'd turn around to look at?

The vertebral arteries pass through bony holes up to 10 times wider than the artery (Johns Hopkins, 2013)
Blood vessels at the base of the head balloon into reservoirs that keep the brain supplied while the head turns

topic.title: How do bees turn flower nectar into honey?

package.title: Why Honey Starts As 80% Water 🐝
package.description:
How do bees make honey? Bees sip flower nectar (up to 80% water) into their honey stomach, add enzymes that split the sugar, pass it mouth to mouth in the hive, then fan it with their wings until it's about 18% water and seal it with wax.

Sources:

https://www.earthdate.org/episodes/how-bees-make-honey
https://localhivehoney.com/blogs/blog/how-much-honey-does-a-bee-make

package.pinned_comment: So which is it: is honey flower juice, or bee spit? 🐝 Tell me your answer!
package.script: Your honey was once 80 percent water, and you'd never guess how bees dried it. It starts with nectar, sugary flower juice. A bee sips it into a second stomach, called the honey stomach. Enzymes from her spit, start chopping the sugar into smaller sugars. Back at the hive, she spits it mouth to mouth, to a house bee, who chews on it for up to 20 minutes. Then it goes into a wax cell. But it's still way too runny. So the bees fan it with their wings, blowing the water away, until it's only about 18 percent water. That's so thick, germs can't grow in it. Then they cap each cell, with wax. One bee makes just a twelfth of a teaspoon, in her whole life. So, is your honey flower juice, or bee spit?
key_facts: Nectar is about 70-80% water (MSU Extension; EarthDate)
Foragers store nectar in the honey stomach (crop) and add invertase, which splits sucrose into glucose and fructose (MSU Extension)
House bees pass nectar back and forth for up to ~20 minutes, then store it in cells (EarthDate)
Bees fan with their wings until honey is ~18% water, too concentrated for microbes; cells are capped with wax (MSU Extension; EarthDate)
A worker bee makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in her lifetime (commonly cited; PBS NOVA via Local Hive)

package.script:
A shrimp smaller than your finger,
fires a bubble almost as hot as the Sun.
But how?
Meet the pistol shrimp.
One claw is huge,
and it cocks open like a gun's hammer.
When it snaps shut,
a plug slams into a socket,
and fires a jet of water,
at about ninety kilometres an hour.
That jet is so fast,
the water behind it rips apart,
into a tiny bubble.
Then the bubble collapses,
in less than a thousandth of a second.
Inside, it hits about four thousand seven hundred degrees,
nearly as hot as the Sun's surface.
It even flashes light.
And that bang isn't the claw.
It's the bubble popping,
one of the loudest sounds in the ocean,

So what animal could beat this shrimp's snap?
key_facts: The pistol shrimp's big claw has a plug that slams into a socket when it snaps shut, firing a water jet (about 90 km/h, ~25 m/s)
The jet is so fast the pressure behind it drops and the water forms a cavitation bubble (Versluis et al., Science 2000)
The bubble collapses in well under a millisecond and its inside is estimated to reach about 4,700°C (over 5,000 K), close to the Sun's surface (~5,500°C)
The collapse emits a brief flash of light (shrimpoluminescence, Lohse et al., Nature 2001)
The snap's sound comes from the bubble collapse, not the claw closing; it is among the loudest sounds in the ocean and can stun small prey

package.script:
Why does your cat's tongue feel like sandpaper?
It's covered in about 300 tiny hooks,
all pointing backwards.
Each hook is a spine called a papilla,
made of keratin,
the same stuff as your fingernails.
But the weirdest part?
The tip of every spine is hollow,
a tiny scoop, like a quill pen.
When a cat licks,

slide down through the fur,
and drop it onto the skin.
That pulls out dirt and tangles,

The papillae reach down through the fur to the skin, delivering saliva there and removing debris and tangles
Grooming evaporation may account for up to a quarter of a cat's cooling; domestic cats spend up to a quarter of their waking hours grooming

package.script: In nineteen-oh-two, a president refused to shoot one bear, and that's why your teddy bear exists. Here's how it all started, on a muddy hunting trip in Mississippi. It's November. President Theodore Roosevelt is out in the swamps, on a bear hunt with the state's governor. After days of searching, Roosevelt hasn't seen a single bear. So his guide, Holt Collier, tracks one down with the hunting dogs, and ties it to a tree. Everyone waits for the president to shoot. But Roosevelt says no. Shooting a tied-up bear isn't fair, so he refuses. A few days later, a cartoonist named Clifford Berryman draws the moment for the Washington Post. In his cartoon, the bear is small and scared, with big round eyes. Readers love it. Berryman keeps drawing that little bear for years, like Roosevelt's furry sidekick. Now jump to Brooklyn, New York. Morris and Rose Michtom run a small shop, selling candy and toys. They see the cartoon, and Rose sews a soft, stuffed bear. They put it in the window, with a sign that says, Teddy's bear. The story goes, they even wrote to Roosevelt to ask if they could use his name. The bears sell out fast. So many people want one, the Michtoms start a whole toy company, called Ideal. But here's the twist. At almost the same time, in Germany, a toy maker called Steiff was making bears too. Margarete Steiff started the company by sewing felt elephants. Her nephew Richard loved sketching bears, and he designed one with arms and legs that move. In nineteen-oh-three, he took it to a big toy fair in Leipzig. At first, almost nobody cared. Then an American buyer ordered three thousand. By nineteen-oh-seven, Steiff was making nine hundred seventy-four thousand bears. So the teddy bear was born twice, on two continents, at almost the same moment. Now look closely at a teddy from back then. Long snout, low forehead, skinny arms. It looks like a real bear. But scientists who measured old teddies found they slowly changed over the years. The snouts got shorter. The foreheads got bigger. The eyes got rounder. Teddy bears started to look like babies. Why? Because people pick the cutest one. Our brains are wired to love baby-like faces, so the cutest bears sold best, year after year. It's evolution, but in a toy shop. Today, teddy bears are everywhere. In two thousand, one Steiff bear, with sapphire and diamond eyes, sold at an auction in Monaco for two point one million dollars. And it's not just kids who love them. In one British survey, about a third of adults said they still sleep with a teddy. All because, more than a hundred twenty years ago, one president wouldn't shoot one bear. package.description:
Why don't hippos get sunburned? Glands under a hippo's skin ooze a clear fluid that turns red, then orange-brown, within minutes; its red and orange pigments (hipposudoric and norhipposudoric acid) soak up UV light like a natural sunscreen, and the red one also stopped bacteria growing in lab tests.

package.script: Hippos sweat red goo, and you'll never see one sunburned. But why? A hippo spends hours in the African sun, with almost no hair to protect it. So its skin fights back. Glands under the skin ooze a thick, clear goo. Within a few minutes, it turns bright red, then a rusty orange-brown. That's why people call it blood sweat. But it's not blood, and it's not really sweat. The color comes from two pigments, one red, one orange. Together, they soak up ultraviolet light, like built-in sunscreen. And the red one does even more. In lab tests, it stopped nasty bacteria from growing. Handy, when rivals leave scratches all over you. So a hippo makes its own sunscreen, and its own antibiotic. If you could sweat any color, which one would you pick?

topic.title: How do penguins keep their feet from freezing?

package.title: Penguins Keep Their Feet at 0°C On Purpose 🐧
package.description:
How do penguins keep their feet from freezing on the ice? Warm blood flowing down their legs runs right beside cold blood coming back up, so heat is swapped before it reaches the feet (countercurrent heat exchange), and the feet stay just above freezing while rocking back on their heels and tail keeps the toes off the ice.

package.pinned_comment: How long do you think YOUR bare toes would last on Antarctic ice? 🧊
package.script:
You'd lose your toes on this ice.
Emperor penguins stand on it for two months.
The secret is in their legs.
Warm blood flowing down to the feet
runs right beside cold blood coming back up.
So the heat jumps across,
like passing a hot potato.
By the time blood reaches the toes,
it's just above freezing.
Cold toes lose very little heat to the ice,
and the warmth goes back into the body.
Feet near zero degrees,
body near thirty-eight.
If the toes get too cold,
the penguin widens its arteries,
and sends down a little more warm blood.
Still chilly?
It rocks back on its heels and stiff tail,
lifting its toes off the ice,
and hunches down,
so belly feathers blanket its feet.
A penguin keeps its feet cold on purpose.
So how long would your toes last out there?

package.description:

package.pinned_comment: Measure yourself tonight and tomorrow morning: how much taller were you? 📏
package.script: You lose one centimeter of height every day, but why? Your spine isn't one solid bone. It's a stack of vertebrae, with twenty-three squishy discs in between. Each disc is like a jelly doughnut, with a soft, watery middle. All day, gravity pushes down on you. Every step and every sit squeezes a little water out, and the discs flatten a tiny bit. Add up all twenty-three, and you've shrunk about a centimeter by bedtime. But when you lie down to sleep, the weight comes off your spine. The discs soak water back up, like little sponges, and by morning, you're tall again. In space, with no gravity, astronauts can grow three percent taller! So tonight, measure yourself before bed, then again when you wake up. Will you be one centimeter taller tomorrow morning?
key_facts: The intervertebral discs between vertebrae compress under load during the day, so people are typically around 1 cm (often quoted up to about 2 cm) shorter by evening (scienceblog; mechse.illinois.edu)
The adult spine has 23 intervertebral discs, each with a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft, water-rich gel centre (nucleus pulposus)
Lying down removes the load and the discs rehydrate overnight, restoring height by morning
Without gravity, astronauts' spines lengthen and they can grow up to about 3% taller in space (Scientific American; Space.com)

package.title: How Do Animals Survive 7 Months Frozen Solid?
package.description:
How do animals survive being frozen solid? Wood frogs freeze with no heartbeat for months, Arctic ground squirrels supercool below zero, Antarctic fish make antifreeze proteins, and tardigrades dry out and wake up decades later.

Sources:

package.pinned_comment: Which trick would you pick to survive the winter: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, or drying out?
package.script: Frozen solid for seven months. No heartbeat. No breathing. You'd be dead. This frog just hops away in spring. So how do animals survive being frozen? Today, four champions of the cold, each with a totally different trick. Meet the wood frog. It lives as far north as Alaska, and it doesn't hide from winter. It just lies down under the leaves, and lets the ice come. The problem with freezing is sharp ice crystals. If they grow inside a cell, they rip it apart like tiny knives. So the frog plays a clever game. As ice touches its skin, its liver floods the body with sugar, up to ten times the normal amount. That sugar soaks into every cell, like a syrup that won't freeze. So the ice can only grow outside the cells, in the spaces in between. Up to sixty percent of the frog turns to ice. No heartbeat. No breath. In Alaska, it can stay like this for as long as seven months. Then spring comes, the ice melts, and the heart starts beating again. Our second champion uses the opposite trick. The Arctic ground squirrel never freezes at all, even when its body drops below zero. Scientists measured one at almost minus three degrees, the coldest body ever found in a mammal. How? It's called supercooling. Water needs a tiny seed to start freezing, like a speck of dust, or a bit of ice. The squirrel's blood is so clean, there's nothing for ice to grow on. So it stays liquid, below freezing. But that's risky. So every few weeks, the squirrel shivers, warms itself back up for a little while, then drops back into the deep cold. Now, dive under the Antarctic ice. The sea here is almost minus two degrees, cold enough to freeze most fish solid. But these Antarctic fish swim around just fine. Their blood is full of antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks in, the proteins grab onto it, and wrap it up so it can't grow. One of their cousins, the icefish, went even further. Its blood has no red cells at all. It's clear, like water. And then there's the toughest of them all. The tardigrade, or water bear, smaller than a grain of sand. When things get bad, it dries itself out, curls into a tiny ball called a tun, and basically pauses its life. In nineteen eighty three, scientists collected moss in Antarctica, and kept it in a freezer at minus twenty. Thirty years later, they thawed it out. Two water bears woke up, and one of them went on to lay nineteen eggs. So why do scientists care? Because we can't do this yet. A donor heart on ice only lasts about four to six hours. Researchers are studying the frog's sugar, and the fish's antifreeze, to keep organs alive for much longer. Four animals, four tricks: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, and drying out. Which one would you pick? Next time, how did a bitter bean become the world's favorite treat, chocolate?
key_facts: Wood frogs: up to ~60% of the body freezes, heart and breathing stop, glucose up to ~10x normal acts as a cryoprotectant; in Alaska up to ~7 months frozen (Audubon)
Arctic ground squirrel: supercools to about -2.9 C, lowest body temperature recorded in a mammal; rewarms every few weeks (UAF)
Antarctic notothenioid fish: seawater about -1.9 C, antifreeze glycoproteins bind ice crystals; icefish have no red blood cells / hemoglobin, colorless blood (Wikipedia: Antarctic fishes)
Tardigrades: moss collected in Antarctica Nov 1983, stored at -20 C, thawed 2014; two revived, one laid 19 eggs (phys.org 2016)
Donor hearts are typically kept on ice for about 4-6 hours

package.pinned_comment: Have you EVER managed to tickle yourself? Tell me how 👇
package.script: Your brain cancels your own tickles before you feel them. But how? Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the order to the cerebellum, at the back of your head. It predicts what the touch will feel like, then turns the feeling down. No surprise, no tickle. When someone else tickles you, there's no prediction. Then the robot added a delay of just two tenths of a second. Suddenly, it felt more ticklish. The prediction was off, so the brain couldn't cancel it. So your own brain blocks the tickle. Can you find a way to outsmart it?

Why does bread go stale, and why is it faster in the fridge? Stale bread isn't mostly dried out: as it cools, its starch slowly packs back into crystals (retrogradation) that squeeze out and lock away water, and that happens fastest just above freezing, so the fridge can stale bread up to about six times faster, while the freezer almost stops it and warming re-melts the crystals for a while.

package.pinned_comment: Fridge, counter or freezer: where does YOUR bread live? 🍞
package.script: Your fridge is wasting your bread. It can go stale six times faster. But why? Fresh bread is soft because of starch. In the oven, starch soaks up water, and its tight crystals melt into a soft gel. But once the bread cools, the starch packs back into crystals. Scientists call it retrogradation. Those crystals squeeze the water out, and lock it away. So the crumb turns hard, even though it's barely dried out. That's why sealed bread still goes stale. And this crystal building runs fastest just above freezing, right at fridge temperature. In the freezer, it almost stops. The fix? Warm stale bread in the oven, and the crystals melt again. It goes soft, almost like fresh, but only for a little while. So, fridge, counter, or freezer: where does your bread live?

package.script: Woodpeckers headbang trees twenty times a second, and you'd be out cold after one. So why don't they get headaches? Each peck stops the head in about a thousandth of a second. That's over a thousand g. For years, people thought the skull was a spongy crash helmet. But in 2022, slow-motion videos showed it barely cushions anything. It's a stiff hammer, because a soft one would hit weaker. The real trick is size. A woodpecker's brain weighs just a few grams, packed so snugly it barely sloshes. Tiny brains handle far bigger hits than ours. Plus, its long tongue bone wraps all the way around its skull, which may help keep things steady. That's up to twelve thousand pecks a day, and not one headache. So what would you headbang twenty times a second?

two things are locked in separate rooms.

like the melanin in your skin.
Scientists think it's a defence,
a brown shield against germs and bugs,
just like a scab on your knee.

package.title: How Chocolate Went From 5,300-Year-Old Bean to Bar
package.description:
The history of chocolate, from cacao beans used 5,300 years ago in the Amazon and the Maya's bitter foamy drink, to Aztec cocoa-bean money, the first chocolate bar in 1847 and the invention of milk chocolate. Plus why chocolate melts in your mouth but not in your hand.

package.script: You could buy a turkey with a hundred cocoa beans. So why did chocolate stop being money, and how did it end up in your hand? This is the story of chocolate. It starts with a tree in the rainforest. The cacao tree grows big, football-shaped pods, right on its trunk. Inside each pod are thirty to fifty seeds, wrapped in sweet white pulp. Those seeds are cocoa beans. Scientists found traces of cacao in pots from the Amazon in Ecuador, about five thousand three hundred years old. Later, the Olmec and the Maya turned the beans into a drink. They roasted them, ground them into paste, and mixed in water, chili, and cornmeal. Then they poured it from high up, from one cup into another, to whip up a thick foam on top. And here's the thing. It wasn't sweet at all. It was bitter, spicy, and very special. The Aztecs loved it so much they used the beans as money. One record from the fifteen hundreds lists prices. A tomato cost one bean. An avocado, three beans. A turkey hen, one hundred. Some people even made fake beans, by stuffing empty shells with mud. Then, in the fifteen hundreds, Spanish explorers carried cacao back across the ocean. The Spanish court tried the bitter drink, and did something new. They added sugar, plus cinnamon and vanilla. Suddenly, Europe was hooked. Fancy chocolate houses opened in London, where rich people sipped it hot. But for almost three hundred years, chocolate was still only a drink. Here's why. A cocoa bean is about half fat, called cocoa butter. Grind the beans, and you get a thick, greasy paste. In eighteen twenty eight, a Dutch chemist named Coenraad van Houten built a press that squeezed out most of that butter. What was left became a dry cake, that could be crushed into cocoa powder. Then in eighteen forty seven, an English company called Fry's flipped the idea. They mixed cocoa powder and sugar with extra melted cocoa butter, and poured it into a mold. It set hard. The first modern chocolate bar. It was still gritty, and a bit bitter. Two Swiss makers fixed that. In eighteen seventy five, Daniel Peter added milk, using milk powder from his neighbor, Henri Nestlé. Milk chocolate was born. Then in eighteen seventy nine, Rodolphe Lindt built a machine called a conche. It rolls warm chocolate back and forth for hours, grinding every bit smaller and smaller, until it turns silky smooth. So what happens today? Farmers cut open the pods and let the beans ferment for about a week. That's where most of the chocolate flavor comes from. Then the beans are dried, roasted, and cracked. It takes around four hundred beans to make one pound of chocolate. And the best trick is in the butter. Cocoa butter melts at about thirty four degrees Celsius, just below the heat inside your mouth. That's why a bar stays solid in your hand, but melts on your tongue. From a bitter drink worth real money, to the bar in your lunchbox. So, would you rather have the drink, or the bar? Next time, how do tiny ants build an underground city for millions of workers?

topic.title: Why do we get goosebumps?

package.title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps? 🥶
package.description:
Why do we get goosebumps? Tiny arrector pili muscles at almost every hair squeeze when you're cold or scared, pulling the hair upright and raising a bump of skin, a leftover from furry ancestors whose fluffed-up fur trapped warm air and made them look bigger.

package.pinned_comment: What gives you goosebumps every single time: a song, a scary movie, or cold air?
package.script:
Your skin hides five million tiny muscles. Why?
Almost every hair on your body
has its own muscle,
called the arrector pili.
When you get cold,
or scared,
your nerves fire one signal,
and they all squeeze at once.
That yanks each hair upright,
and pushes up a bump of skin.
That's a goosebump.
For a furry animal, it's a superpower.
Standing fur traps a layer of warm air,
like a puffy winter coat.
And a scared cat puffs up,
so it looks bigger.
But we lost most of our fur,
so now we just get bumps.
Even a song can trigger them,
because big feelings fire the same nerves.
And in mice, scientists found
those nerves wake up hair stem cells,
to grow thicker fur in the cold.
So what gives you goosebumps?
key_facts: The body has about 5 million hair follicles, and almost every body hair has a tiny arrector pili muscle attached
Cold or fear triggers the sympathetic nervous system, which makes the arrector pili muscles contract
The contraction pulls the hair upright and raises a small bump of skin: a goosebump
In furry mammals, raised fur traps a layer of insulating air and makes the animal look bigger to threats
Strong emotions, such as from music, can trigger the same nervous response
A 2020 Harvard study in mice found the sympathetic nerves tied to these muscles also activate hair follicle stem cells to grow new hair in prolonged cold

package.script:
A dead flamingo can stand on one leg.
Why can't you?
In 2017, scientists in Atlanta tested it.
They propped up a flamingo body,
and it balanced on one leg,
with no muscles working at all.
Here's the trick.
That bendy joint isn't a knee.
It's the ankle.
The real knee is hidden up in the feathers.
When a flamingo lifts one leg,
it shifts its body,
so its weight sits right over the foot.
That weight pushes the joints into a locked position,
like a folding chair clicking open.
No muscles needed, just gravity.
Live flamingos even sway less
when they're fast asleep.
But on two legs,
the dead bird couldn't stay up.
For a flamingo, one leg is the lazy way to stand.
For you, it's a muscle workout.
So how long can you stand on one leg?

topic.title: Why does your stomach growl?

package.title: Why Your Stomach Growls Every 2 Hours
package.description:
Why does your stomach growl, and why is it loudest when it's empty? Your gut is a muscle tube that squeezes food, liquid and gas along in waves (peristalsis); when it's empty there's nothing to muffle the sound, and every one to two hours a cleaning wave sweeps leftovers and bacteria down the gut, rumbling for 10 to 20 minutes until you eat.

package.pinned_comment: When did your stomach growl at the WORST possible moment? Exam, meeting, silent library?
package.script: Your empty stomach growls every two hours until you eat. But why won't it stop? Your gut is one long muscle tube, and its walls squeeze in waves. That's called peristalsis. They push food, liquid and gas along, about three squeezes a minute in your stomach. After a meal, food muffles the sound. But empty? It's mostly gas and air, so every squeeze echoes like a drum. When you've been empty a while, a big cleaning wave kicks in. It sweeps leftover food and bacteria down the whole gut. It rumbles for ten to twenty minutes, then comes back every one to two hours, until you eat again. The ancient Greeks called it borborygmi, which means rumbling. So that growl isn't just hunger. Cats often shine green, Siamese cats often yellow; riboflavin or zinc in the tapetum and retinal pigment affect the colour (NPR).

package.script: Your cat's purr is a twitch, twenty-five times a second. But how? Deep in the throat sits the voice box, with a tiny gap called the glottis. A signal from the brain makes the muscles around it twitch, snapping that gap open and shut. Air rushes in, and the gap chops it into bursts. Air flows out, and it chops it again. That's why a purr just keeps going. In twenty twenty-three, scientists found another clue: tiny pads inside the vocal folds, which may help a small cat hit such a low note. Bobcats and cheetahs purr too, but lions and tigers don't seem to. And a purr doesn't always mean happy. Cats also purr at the vet, or when they're hurt. So when yours starts twitching away, do you think it's happy, or worried?

package.pinned_comment: Which job would you pick in the ant city: leaf hauler, bodyguard, fungus gardener, or trash duty?
package.script: Ants built farms fifty million years before you, and you'd never spot them. And right now, under a rainforest floor, there's an ant city with millions of citizens, thousands of rooms, farms, garbage dumps, and its own air conditioning. So what actually happens inside a leafcutter ant city? It starts up here, on the road. Leafcutter ants march along forest trails in long green parades. Each worker slices off a piece of leaf with her jaws, then hauls it home, carrying up to ten times her own weight. That's like you jogging home with a cow on your back. But look closer. There's a tiny ant riding on top of that leaf. She's the bodyguard. Tiny flies try to lay eggs in the carriers' heads, so this little passenger fends them off. Because in this city, everybody has a job, and your size is your job description. The tiniest ants, called minims, have heads less than a millimeter wide. They look after the babies and the gardens. Medium ants are the foragers you just met. And the giants are the soldiers, with heads up to seven millimeters wide. Now, follow the leaves underground. Here's the twist. They don't really eat them. They'll sip a little sap, but the leaf is just fertilizer. Smaller ants snip each piece into tiny bits. Gardeners crush those bits into pellets, add a drop of their own poop, and press it all into a giant spongy garden. What grows there is a fungus. That's the real food. It feeds babies and adults, and they've been passing this crop down for millions of years. But every farmer has a weed problem. A rival fungus can wreck the whole crop. So the ants wear a white powder on their bodies. That powder is bacteria, and it makes antibiotics that hold the weed back. Infected patches get chopped out and dragged away, which brings us to the trash. Waste goes to separate garbage rooms, some big enough for you to stand inside. The workers there are mostly older ants, kept apart from everyone else. A city this big has one more problem. Breathing. All that fungus and all those ants make carbon dioxide. The ants can handle it. Their fungus can't. So one species builds chimneys. When wind blows across the mound, it pulls stale air out of the top holes, and fresh air gets drawn in. Those turrets can boost the airflow up to ten times. No fans. No electricity. So who started all this? The queen. She can live up to fifteen years, and by one estimate, lay a hundred fifty million eggs. But her story begins with one flight. A young queen leaves home with a tiny pellet of fungus in her mouth. That's her whole inheritance. She digs in, seals herself underground, and plants it. Only about two and a half percent build a colony that lasts. But the winners can end up with seven thousand rooms, more than twenty feet deep. So next time you see a leaf walking across the ground, remember where it's going. It's headed to a farm far older than us. Next up, another insect city, where workers talk by dancing. How does a honeybee hive work?

package.script: Your popcorn explodes at about 4 times, your car tire's pressure. Every kernel hides a bit of water, about 14 percent, packed in soft starch, locked inside a hard shell called the hull. Heat it up, and that water turns to steam. topic.title: Why does hair turn grey?

package.title: Why Do 91% of Us Have Grey Hair by 65?
package.description:
Why does hair turn grey? Melanocyte stem cells in the hair follicle stop moving and get stuck, so fewer colour cells make melanin, a finding from a 2023 study in mice.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/health/ageing/why-does-hair-turn-gray
https://www.npr.org/2023/04/21/1171110131/gray-hair-stem-cells-reversible

package.pinned_comment: If scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey or go back?
package.script: Your grey hairs start with stuck cells, tiny ones, at your roots. Hair gets its colour from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. They sit at the bottom of each follicle, and inject colour as the hair grows. But those cells need replacing, and that's the job of stem cells. In mice, scientists found these stem cells commute, moving up and down the follicle. Moving is how they get the signal to make colour. But as hair ages, more of them stop. They get stuck in a spot called the bulge. In plucked mouse hair, stuck cells jumped, from fifteen percent to nearly fifty. Stuck cells can't make new colour cells. Less melanin means grey, no melanin means white. By your early sixties, about ninety-one percent of people have some grey. So if scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey, or go back?
key_facts: Melanin made by melanocytes at the base of the follicle gives hair its colour (Live Science)

package.title: How Do 60,000 Bees Run a Hive With No Boss?
package.description:
How does a honeybee hive work with no one in charge? See how the queen, drones and workers split the jobs, why comb is built from hexagons, how the waggle dance gives directions, and how bees heat and cool the hive.

package.pinned_comment: Which hive job would you want: cleaner, nurse, builder, guard, or forager?
package.script: Sixty thousand bees, no boss, and you'd never guess how they run it. This hive builds perfect rooms, runs its own heating and cooling, and shares maps by dancing. So how does a honeybee hive actually work? Let's start with the queen. She sounds like the boss, but she doesn't give orders. Her real job is eggs. At her peak, she can lay up to fifteen hundred a day. That's about one egg every minute, all day and all night. Around her are a few hundred males, called drones. They're only here to mate with a new queen. And when the cold comes in fall, the workers shove them out the door. Everyone else is a worker, and every worker is female. A queen and a worker can start as the same kind of egg. The difference is food. A future queen gets loads of royal jelly, and a worker gets far less. Now, a summer worker only lives about six weeks, and she changes careers the whole way through. Day one, she's a cleaner, polishing her own cell. Around day five, she's a nurse, feeding the babies. Around day twelve, wax glands on her belly switch on, so she turns builder. Around day fifteen, she can guard the door. And after about three weeks, she finally goes outside, to spend the rest of her life hunting flowers. Wax is seriously expensive. It takes about eight pounds of honey, to make one pound of wax. So the hive can't waste a drop. Circles leave gaps. Squares and triangles fit, but they use more wall. Hexagons give you the most room, for the least wax. People suspected that for centuries, but a mathematician only proved it in nineteen ninety-nine. Bees got there first, with no math at all. Now, the coolest trick in the hive. A forager finds flowers a long way off. How does she tell her sisters, in the pitch dark, with no words? She dances. She runs in a straight line, shaking her body, loops back, and does it again. The angle of that run is the direction. Straight up means fly toward the sun. Sixty degrees to the left, means sixty degrees left of the sun. And the waggle's length is the distance. A waggle of about two and a half seconds, means flowers over a mile and a half away. Cracking that code won Karl von Frisch, a Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three. The babies are picky. They need to stay close to ninety-five degrees Fahrenheit. Too cold? Workers shiver their flight muscles, without flapping, and turn into tiny heaters. Too hot? They carry in water, spread it on the comb, and fan it with their wings. As it evaporates, the hive cools down. That's air conditioning, powered by bees. And in winter, they don't hibernate. Below about fifty-seven degrees, they pull into a tight ball around the queen, and burn honey to make heat. That's why they store all that honey. It's their winter fuel. So no single bee knows the plan. Each one just follows simple rules. But put sixty thousand together, and you get something that acts like one giant animal. Next up, why does cilantro taste like soap, to some people?

At her peak, she can lay up to fifteen hundred a day.

12
00:00:25,790 --> 00:00:27,570
That's about one egg every minute,

13
00:00:27,870 --> 00:00:29,250
all day and all night.

14
00:00:29,800 --> 00:00:31,880
Around her are a few hundred males,

15
00:00:32,180 --> 00:00:33,160
called drones.

16
00:00:33,710 --> 00:00:35,830
They're only here to mate with a new queen.

17
00:00:36,380 --> 00:00:38,110
And when the cold comes in fall,

18
00:00:38,410 --> 00:00:40,280
the workers shove them out the door.

19
00:00:40,830 --> 00:00:42,450
Everyone else is a worker,

20
00:00:42,750 --> 00:00:44,420
and every worker is female.

21
00:00:44,970 --> 00:00:48,410
A queen and a worker can start as the same kind of egg.

22
00:00:48,960 --> 00:00:50,260
The difference is food.

23
00:00:50,810 --> 00:00:53,390
A future queen gets loads of royal jelly,

24
00:00:53,690 --> 00:00:55,410
and a worker gets far less.

25
00:00:55,960 --> 00:00:58,980
Now, a summer worker only lives about six weeks,

26
00:00:59,280 --> 00:01:01,640
and she changes careers the whole way through.

27
00:01:02,190 --> 00:01:03,640
Day one, she's a cleaner,

28
00:01:03,940 --> 00:01:05,270
polishing her own cell.

29
00:01:05,820 --> 00:01:07,580
Around day five, she's a nurse,

30
00:01:07,880 --> 00:01:09,070
feeding the babies.

31
00:01:09,620 --> 00:01:13,120
Around day twelve, wax glands on her belly switch on,

32
00:01:13,420 --> 00:01:14,710
so she turns builder.

33
00:01:15,260 --> 00:01:17,910
Around day fifteen, she can guard the door.

34
00:01:18,460 --> 00:01:20,020
And after about three weeks,

35
00:01:20,320 --> 00:01:21,990
she finally goes outside,

36
00:01:22,290 --> 00:01:24,860
to spend the rest of her life hunting flowers.

37
00:01:25,410 --> 00:01:27,140
Wax is seriously expensive.

38
00:01:27,690 --> 00:01:29,590
It takes about eight pounds of honey,

39
00:01:29,890 --> 00:01:31,410
to make one pound of wax.

40
00:01:31,960 --> 00:01:33,910
So the hive can't waste a drop.

41
00:01:34,460 --> 00:01:35,760
Circles leave gaps.

42
00:01:36,310 --> 00:01:37,860
Squares and triangles fit,

43
00:01:38,160 --> 00:01:39,590
but they use more wall.

44
00:01:40,140 --> 00:01:41,990
Hexagons give you the most room,

45
00:01:42,290 --> 00:01:43,410
for the least wax.

46
00:01:43,960 --> 00:01:45,990
People suspected that for centuries,

47
00:01:46,290 --> 00:01:50,010
but a mathematician only proved it in nineteen ninety-nine.

48
00:01:50,560 --> 00:01:53,240
Bees got there first, with no math at all.

49
00:01:53,790 --> 00:01:55,680
Now, the coolest trick in the hive.

50
00:01:56,230 --> 00:01:58,790
A forager finds flowers a long way off.

51
00:01:59,340 --> 00:02:00,880
How does she tell her sisters,

52
00:02:01,180 --> 00:02:03,010
in the pitch dark, with no words?

53
00:02:03,560 --> 00:02:04,450
She dances.

54
00:02:05,000 --> 00:02:06,530
She runs in a straight line,

55
00:02:06,830 --> 00:02:07,960
shaking her body,

56
00:02:08,260 --> 00:02:09,100
loops back,

57
00:02:09,400 --> 00:02:10,470
and does it again.

58
00:02:11,020 --> 00:02:13,270
The angle of that run is the direction.

59
00:02:13,820 --> 00:02:15,840
Straight up means fly toward the sun.

60
00:02:16,390 --> 00:02:17,960
Sixty degrees to the left,

61
00:02:18,260 --> 00:02:20,410
means sixty degrees left of the sun.

62
00:02:20,960 --> 00:02:22,960
And the waggle's length is the distance.

63
00:02:23,510 --> 00:02:25,680
A waggle of about two and a half seconds,

64
00:02:25,980 --> 00:02:28,550
means flowers over a mile and a half away.

65
00:02:29,100 --> 00:02:31,450
Cracking that code won Karl von Frisch,

66
00:02:31,750 --> 00:02:34,390
a Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three.

67
00:02:34,940 --> 00:02:36,250
The babies are picky.

68
00:02:36,800 --> 00:02:39,910
They need to stay close to ninety-five degrees Fahrenheit.

69
00:02:40,460 --> 00:02:41,310
Too cold?

70
00:02:41,860 --> 00:02:43,900
Workers shiver their flight muscles,

71
00:02:44,200 --> 00:02:45,240
without flapping,

72
00:02:45,540 --> 00:02:47,300
and turn into tiny heaters.

73
00:02:47,850 --> 00:02:48,660
Too hot?

74
00:02:49,210 --> 00:02:50,430
They carry in water,

75
00:02:50,730 --> 00:02:51,950
spread it on the comb,

76
00:02:52,250 --> 00:02:53,750
and fan it with their wings.

77
00:02:54,300 --> 00:02:56,750
As it evaporates, the hive cools down.

78
00:02:57,300 --> 00:02:58,590
That's air conditioning,

79
00:02:58,890 --> 00:03:00,090
powered by bees.

80
00:03:00,640 --> 00:03:02,690
And in winter, they don't hibernate.

81
00:03:03,240 --> 00:03:05,370
Below about fifty-seven degrees,

82
00:03:05,670 --> 00:03:07,930
they pull into a tight ball around the queen,

83
00:03:08,230 --> 00:03:09,860
and burn honey to make heat.

84
00:03:10,410 --> 00:03:12,300
That's why they store all that honey.

85
00:03:12,850 --> 00:03:14,200
It's their winter fuel.

86
00:03:14,750 --> 00:03:16,630
So no single bee knows the plan.

87
00:03:17,180 --> 00:03:19,330
Each one just follows simple rules.

88
00:03:19,880 --> 00:03:21,660
But put sixty thousand together,

89
00:03:21,960 --> 00:03:24,890
and you get something that acts like one giant animal.

90
00:03:25,440 --> 00:03:28,250
Next up, why does cilantro taste like soap,

91
00:03:28,550 --> 00:03:29,580
to some people?

package.title: Why Do Pigeons Bob Their Heads 5 Times a Second? 🐦
package.description:
Why do pigeons bob their heads when they walk? The head thrusts forward, then holds still in space while the body catches up, which keeps the bird's view of the world steady, and a 1978 treadmill experiment showed the bobbing stops when the surroundings don't move.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/why-pigeons-bob-heads.html
https://www.snopes.com/articles/352787/why-do-pigeons-bob-their-heads/
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/why-do-pigeons-bob-their-heads-when-they-walk.html

package.pinned_comment: Next time you see a pigeon, watch the head: can you catch it standing still?
package.script: Pigeon heads never bob, you've been watching them freeze in midair. Watch one walk, the head shoots forward, about two inches. That's the thrust. Then it stops dead, locked in place, while the body walks underneath it. That's the hold. Then forward again, five to eight times every second. But why bother? In nineteen seventy-eight, scientists in Canada put a pigeon on a treadmill. Its legs kept walking, but the world around it stayed still, and the bobbing stopped. So it isn't about balance, it's about what the bird sees. Holding its head still keeps the view steady, like a camera on a tripod, while the world slides past. Chickens and cranes do it too. So next time you see a pigeon, watch the head. Is it bobbing, or standing still?
key_facts: The head thrusts forward about 2 inches relative to the body, then holds still in space while the body moves forward (Michael Land via Live Science; Journal of Comparative Physiology A 2007 via Snopes).
This happens on average five to eight times a second while walking (Aaron Blaisdell via Live Science).

In 1978, researchers at Queen's University in Canada found the bobbing stopped when a pigeon walked on a treadmill with stationary surroundings, pointing to a visual response rather than balance (Live Science, Snopes).
Chickens and cranes also head-bob (Snopes).
